body.text: The debate over air power often becomes a choice between quantity and quality. But India needs both

The Indian Air Force’s most urgent challenge is not a lack of ambition or strategic vision. It is the erosion of numbers. With fighter strength at roughly 29 squadrons against an authorised 42, the IAF is operating with a margin that is becoming increasingly difficult to sustain. Air Chief Marshal A.P. Singh’s recent warning that India needs to induct 36–40 fighter aircraft every year should therefore be seen not as an aspirational target but as the minimum required to arrest further decline and begin rebuilding strength.

The strategic environment makes this particularly urgent. India continues to face the possibility of a two-front contingency involving China and Pakistan, while both adversaries are modernising their air forces. China’s rapid progress in stealth technology and reports of potential Chinese fifth-generation aircraft being supplied to Pakistan point to a changing regional balance. India cannot afford to allow its numerical disadvantage to widen while its competitors acquire new capabilities.

The immediate priority must therefore be simple: arrest and reverse the fighter-squadron shortfall. The debate over air power often becomes a choice between quantity and quality. That is misleading. India needs both. Advanced aircraft, precision weapons, sensors and networks provide qualitative advantages, but they cannot compensate indefinitely for insufficient numbers. Aircraft require maintenance, training and rotation. Operations generate fatigue and attrition. A force that is too small has limited surge capacity and reduced flexibility across multiple theatres.

This is why the delays surrounding the Tejas Mk-1A are strategically significant. India had hoped that the indigenous fighter would become the foundation of a sustained production ecosystem. Instead, delays involving GE F404 engines, radar and missile integration and software certification have slowed induction. The principle that “technology delayed is technology denied” is particularly relevant here. Every aircraft that arrives years late represents combat capability that was unavailable when it was needed.

The immediate objective should therefore be to remove every remaining bottleneck and enable HAL to reach production rates of 20 or more Tejas aircraft annually. The IAF has several streams through which it can begin rebuilding squadron strength. The first is the Tejas Mk-1A, whose production must be accelerated. The second is the proposed Multi-Role Fighter Aircraft programme, involving roughly 114 aircraft and potentially centred on the Rafale, with substantial production in India. Once established, this could provide another stream of around 12 aircraft annually. The additional Su-30 aircraft already envisaged would provide further reinforcement.

If these programmes proceed on schedule, India could approach the 35-40 aircraft-a-year induction rate identified by the Air Chief. But that requires procurement, industrial production, engines, certification and logistics to be treated as one integrated national-security problem rather than separate bureaucratic processes. At the same time, the existing fleet must be kept combat-ready. Su-30s, Rafales, Mirage-2000s, Jaguars and Tejas Mk-1s need reliable spares, high serviceability and rapid integration of indigenous weapons such as the Astra family. Numbers matter only when aircraft are available for operations.

India’s long-term answer must remain the indigenous Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft. AMCA is more than another fighter programme: it is a test of whether India can develop an advanced combat-aircraft ecosystem rather than remain dependent on foreign suppliers. But strategic patience cannot become strategic paralysis.

If AMCA timelines slip substantially, India will eventually have to consider interim options, including the Russian Su-57 offer. Such an option would involve difficult questions concerning cost, technology access, interoperability and industrial benefits. Nevertheless, the choice should be made on the basis of strategic necessity rather than institutional inertia.

Modern air warfare is increasingly about systems rather than individual platforms. Sensors, electronic warfare, missiles, communications, command-and-control networks, training and doctrine can be as important as the aircraft itself. India therefore needs an integrated combat system rather than a fixation on individual platforms.

Unmanned systems and loitering munitions will increasingly shape the battlefield. For the IAF, they can provide surveillance, targeting, persistence and strike capabilities while complementing manned aircraft. But they should not become an excuse for accepting inadequate fighter numbers.

The future battlefield will involve manned aircraft, unmanned systems, missiles, electronic warfare and air-defence networks operating together. The objective should be integration rather than creating parallel structures that fragment command. Humans are likely to remain in the decision loop for the foreseeable future, particularly for high-end combat operations. India’s air-power challenge extends beyond fighter procurement. The IAF needs an integrated aerospace architecture in which sensors, shooters and command networks operate seamlessly.

Indigenous weapons such as Astra, Akash and BrahMos need to be produced and integrated rapidly. Artificial intelligence should augment human decision-making. Integrated air and missile defence must keep pace with increasingly complex threats involving aircraft, cruise missiles, ballistic missiles and unmanned systems.

Self-reliance cannot simply mean announcing indigenous programmes. It must mean the ability to produce engines, components, weapons and platforms in sufficient quantities and within strategically relevant timelines.

India’s defence-industrial ambitions have made significant progress, but the next challenge is scale and speed. Self-reliance cannot simply mean announcing indigenous programmes. It must mean the ability to produce engines, components, weapons and platforms in sufficient quantities and within strategically relevant timelines. The experience of the Tejas programme demonstrates the problem. A largely indigenous aircraft can still be constrained by imported engines or delays in certification and systems integration.

India therefore needs both indigenous development and carefully structured international partnerships, particularly in areas such as aero-engines and next-generation technologies. Foreign collaboration should strengthen domestic industrial capacity rather than create another cycle of dependence.

The IAF’s priorities should therefore be sequenced clearly. First, arrest the decline in fighter numbers. Accelerate Tejas Mk-1A production, move the MRFA programme rapidly into execution, induct additional Su-30s and maintain the existing fleet at high availability.

Second, protect qualitative capability. Modern weapons, sensors, electronic warfare, communications and network integration must ensure that every additional aircraft adds more than a single platform to India’s combat power.

Third, push AMCA aggressively while establishing clear milestones and decision points. If delays become strategically unacceptable, India should consider interim fifth-generation options rather than wait indefinitely.

Fourth, expand unmanned systems, artificial intelligence, integrated air defence and network-centric warfare as force multipliers. The sequencing matters. India cannot build its future air force while allowing its present one to hollow out.

For too long, delays in defence acquisition have been treated as bureaucratic inconveniences. In an increasingly contested regional environment, they are becoming strategic liabilities. Air power will remain a central instrument through which India converts economic and diplomatic weight into strategic influence. But influence ultimately rests on credible capability. And credible air power requires both technological sophistication and sufficient numbers. India must therefore move from managing scarcity to rebuilding strength-and do so before the strategic environment leaves it with fewer choices.
This commentary originally appeared in Hindustan Times.
